chunks: From him, from al-Abbas ibn Ma'ruf, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from some of our companions, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
The hunter is not required to shorten his prayer for three days, and if he exceeds three days, it becomes obligatory (for him to complete).

The ruling in these two narrations applies to one whose hunting is for his food and the food of his dependents; as for one whose hunting is for amusement, it is not permissible for him to shorten (his prayer), as we have clarified.
It was transmitted from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him)
That the hunter shortens (his prayer) as long as he is on the main road; when he deviates from the main road, he completes (his prayer); and when he returns to it, he shortens (his prayer).

key_terms.صَاحِبُ الصَّيْدِ: The hunter / one engaged in hunting

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on shortening prayers while hunting in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi contextualizes this ruling within the broader jurisprudence of travel, distinguishing between hunting for sustenance, which permits shortening prayers for up to three days, and hunting for amusement, which does not. The second narration clarifies that the legal status of 'travel' (and thus the right to qasr) is contingent upon being on the main road (al-jaddah), requiring full prayer upon deviation and resuming shortening upon return. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the physical location and purpose of the journey in determining ritual obligations.
